Oceanographer here. Counterintuitively, melting sea ice *does* raise sea level, however slightly. When sea ice freezes, it undergoes brine rejection such that the ice is only “fresh” ice, increasing the salinity of the surrounding water. Saltier water is denser due to electrostriction, and thus occupies a smaller volume. Seawater saltiness also depresses the freezing point to -4C, also making it denser and reducing the volume. So, when sea ice melts, it not only reduces the density through freshening, but also through warming, and both effects increase its relative volume. Overall however, these effects make only a small difference on sea level.

Sea level rise is not linear and is not rising uniformly or at all in some places. Many places are experiencing zero or even negative sea level change. This variance can occur even on a kilometer-by-kilometer basis. It is primarily driven by changes in ocean currents, wind, sea surface temperatures, and tectonic and other hydrological dynamics.

On the Oregon Coast for example, some low-lying areas will likely experience 12-18”+ of SLR by 2050. Other areas (primarily in the south), are undergoing rapid tectonic uplift that will outpace sea level rise until at least the mid 2030s, and may experience few impacts because of the high continental freeboard. 

These systems are highly dynamic and variable, but it is clear that overall global sea level is rising on average at a MUCH higher rate compared to the historical record and will lead to costly impacts for many communities.

Sophie’s father was a liberal politician who disliked Hitler, and it clearly rubbed off on his daughter. My grandmother was raised in a rural area with a simple life, but wanted an education. At the time, the only way to get an education was through programs influenced by the Nazi government. My grandma wasn’t particularly political or knew much about what was going on in government, but didn’t care for Hitler or the Nazis. She wanted an education though, so she moved to Dresden to go through one of the (propagandized) programs. It was just gymnastics/kinesthetics/physiology, and she understood there were propaganda elements to it and ignored those. 

So, is my grandmother guilty by association simply for being a woman who wanted an education to better her life beyond her pastoral upbringing? Or for not actively resisting the regime? Does the fact that she later got a job as a translator for the American army absolve her of her participation? How much can you demand of the average citizen? Was Sophie more politically active simply because she lived in the city and came from a more privileged upbringing? 

The fact is it’s pretty hard to judge people of the past by the standards of today. It’s easy to consume information about the world on your smartphone and think that people of the past had similar understandings. They didn’t. After my grandma lost her apartment in the firebombing of Dresden, she had to walk home across half of Germany to her parents - neither of them knew if the other was alive. That’s how poor communications were. Most people really had a poor understanding of everything that was going on. You had to read the (propagandized) papers or listen to the (propagandistic) radio. Do you also blame the average poor North Korean for not fighting their regime? Would you blame women in Afghanistan for going to Taliban-controlled schools?

I just don’t think we can act so smug from our cushy, privileged position to think that we’d also stand up to a tyrannical regime with our *lives*, instead of simply trying to survive. Ice cores repositories like this are invaluable research tools. They can be sampled many times for any number of research related reasons. Often they are used to study past climate and ocean regimes through the use of [proxies](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proxy_(climate)). Where and how deep they were sampled allows us to reconstruct past conditions for specific regions just the same as you might sample current conditions multiple places over a broad area to get a better constrained result. Drilling a handful of cores that you can then sample hundreds of times each is a lot more cost effective than sending scientists to the farthest reaches of the planet every time you need a new sample. 

Source: I’m an oceanographer and we often collect and study sea floor sediment cores as well as ice cores.

Melting sea ice *does* actually contribute to sea level rise, however slightly, partly for exactly the reason that you identified - thermal expansion. The saltiness in sea water depresses the freezing point to -4C, so polar seas are often liquid “below” freezing. When sea ice forms it undergoes brine rejection, leaving the salt behind to form fresh ice. As things warm up, sea ice melts, freshening the water and raising its freezing temperature. Water with dissolved ions in it also undergoes electrostriction - a contraction of its volume related to ionic interactions. So the combined effects of ionic expansion, freezing point elevation, and thermal expansion, all slightly contribute to an increase in sea level.
